name: Carex

project_scope.study_context: Hays County and 24-county Central Texas target-zone visual ID
project_scope.native_range_note: Per-species native statuses remain PROVISIONAL / unverified for strict county certification; do not infer PASS from species inclusion.
project_scope.media_note: Six existing licensed genus presentation anchors (five real photographs and one historic botanical drawing); three institutional photos rights-unverified and tetrastachya has no installed media.

look_here_first: First decide whether you're looking at a CAREX flowering spike: several scales along one or more spikes, often terminal staminate and lower pistillate spikes. Then examine ONE ripe female unit with a hand lens: the seed-like ACHENE sits INSIDE a sac called the PERIGYNIUM, protected by a separate pistillate SCALE. Notice SPIKE ARRANGEMENT (drooping? rounded? dense?), leaf width/cross-section and the shape of the perigynium BEAK before naming the species. A triangular stem is not a final ID.

genus_diagnostics.perigynium: The genus-defining feature is a thin sac or bladder called a PERIGYNIUM enveloping a female flower and later the single ACHENE (dry, one-seeded fruit). A separate pistillate SCALE lies outside the perigynium. Count veins, look for wings and fine hairs, and inspect the beak at its tip. Achenes are not openly exposed as in most Cyperus.
genus_diagnostics.flower_spikes: Look for distinct flowering SPIKES with reduced flowers under scales. In many Carex, male/staminate spike(s) occur toward the tip and female/pistillate spikes lower down; other Carex have mixed-sex spikes. Shape ranges from drooping loose spikes to many dense narrow fruiting heads. Never treat one pattern as universal.
genus_diagnostics.stems_and_sheaths: Often solid triangular CULMS, but stem shape is only a clue. Leaves arise from mostly CLOSED sheaths and have a sheath-blade junction with a LIGULE. Photograph the culm base, sheath mouth and leaf cross-section on the same plant.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Blades often long and narrow, with two side ridges or a V-shaped fold, but widths range from very thin Texas/cedar sedges to broader Cherokee and Emory sedges. Inspect blade width with a mm scale, midrib and margin roughness; habit alone is not species proof.
genus_diagnostics.achene_and_beak: Each female flower matures one small ACHENE inside its PERIGYNIUM. The sac may be beaked, toothed, winged, inflated, veined, flat or rounded in cross-section. Dissection and 1–2 mm macro photos are often necessary for species certainty.
genus_diagnostics.habitat: The reviewed ten range from dry limestone canyon/cedar woodland to mesic forest, prairies, seeps and wet bottomlands. Moisture and habitat help build a shortlist but are not replacement morphology.

shared_traits: Cyperaceae family: spikelets with highly reduced flowers under scales and dry one-seeded fruits, commonly solid sedge culms and closed sheaths.
Carex genus: each female flower/fruit is wrapped in a PERIGYNIUM, unlike most Cyperus and Eleocharis.
Subgroups vary widely: terminal male + separate female spikes, mixed spikes, winged sac, long beaks and dense fruiting heads occur in different Carex species.
priority: 1. SEE the whole flowering/fruiting plant and whether spikes are drooping, separate, round, or tightly packed.
2. SPOT one perigynium, then peel it back to reveal the single achene. Do not confuse a pistillate scale with the sac.
3. NAME the ligule, closed sheath, leaf blade, spike and beaked perigynium using close shots.
4. COMPARE the canyon pair (edwardsiana/planostachys), drooping woodland pair (cherokeensis/blanda), wetland pair (crus-corvi/emoryi) and winged C. tetrastachya.
5. REMEMBER: 'Carex carries its fruit in a little bag.' Do not diagnose species from stem edges or garden habit.
warnings: Genus includes many lineages; shared genus definition does NOT mean all species have a terminal male spike.
Most existing photo cards are provisional whole-plant faces. Feature-level measured macros are still absent.
Institutional UT voucher photos for edwardsiana, microdonta and perdentata have reuse rights unverified; no new genus reuse till cleared.
Taxonomic native-range certification must remain separate from visual gallery admission.

comparison_cards.title: Broad-leaved woodland sedges: Cherokee vs Blanda
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Count spikes and inspect DROOP. Cherokee sedge usually has several conspicuously arching or drooping long female spikes, while blanda has fewer shorter separated spikes.

field_matrix.cherokeensis: Many (often 4–12) long lateral pistillate spikes, low ones may droop
field_matrix.blanda: Often 3–4 shorter female spikes below one terminal staminate spike
Tufted or loose woodland, broad flat foliage

field_matrix.crus_corvi: Dense branching cylindrical fruiting head with conspicuous long perigynium beaks
field_matrix.emoryi: Several elongated separate lateral female spikes and upper male spikes

quick_key.if: Green tufts on dry calcareous cedar/oak slope, small plant
quick_key.then: Try C. planostachys vs C. edwardsiana. Photograph culm bases, leaf cross-sections and spike spacing.

quick_key.if: Strong purple-red bases, 3–5 separate spaced small spikes in limestone ravine
quick_key.then: C. edwardsiana possibility; exact-species licensed photo of this character needed.

quick_key.if: Broad woodland leaves with several noticeably DROOPING female spikes
quick_key.then: C. cherokeensis; confirm number, shape and perigynium.

quick_key.if: Loose woodland 3–4 shorter female spikes under terminal male
quick_key.then: C. blanda; confirm live photo and fruit.

quick_key.if: Wetland, extremely dense spiny narrow cylindrical fruiting head
quick_key.then: C. crus-corvi, long-beaked perigynia; view true existing head photo.

quick_key.if: Wet bank, tall spreading from rhizomes, separate elongated pistillate spikes
quick_key.then: C. emoryi, photograph fruiting stem (current photo mainly ligule).

quick_key.if: Low fine tuft, very narrow 1–1.7 mm leaves and tiny compact spikes
quick_key.then: C. texensis; not enough without a mature spike close-up.

quick_key.if: Spring fruiting with silvery broad WHITE-WINGED flat perigynia, 2–4 separate round spikes
quick_key.then: C. tetrastachya; request same-taxon verified source, no current installed image.

quick_key.if: Meadow loose oblong fruiting spikes, long-beaked ~1.4–1.8 mm with conspicuous teeth
quick_key.then: C. perdentata; exact fruit macro with ruler needed.

quick_key.if: Plump short-beaked ~0.3–0.9 mm perigynia, wet open site
quick_key.then: C. microdonta; verify structure with magnifier, rights-cleared close-up needed.

visual_comparison.title: Carex: ten sedges, same genus — very different plant parts
visual_comparison.subtitle: Five actual exact-species real photos plus one public-domain botanical illustration, physically present in canonical species folders. Three UT voucher images have unverified reuse and are not copied into this genus; C. tetrastachya has no installed photo. Species identification still requires fruiting perigynia and achenes.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: Carex = a female fruit inside a PERIGYNIUM ('little bag') + a separate outer SCALE. Then compare spike architecture, beak, wings, basal sheath and blades.

part_examples.title: 1 · SPOT the sheath-blade junction
part_examples.look_for: At the point where the vertical green BLADE leaves its pale enclosing SHEATH, find the small transparent membranous LIGULE. It is a REAL Carex ligule example, not a grass collar. The photographed fingers give useful scale.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The grass-versus-sedge distinction is not a ligule/no-ligule rule. Check the floral units for family identity.

part_examples.title: 2 · Compare a woodland spike
part_examples.look_for: Several separate narrow spikes curve and droop from tall woodland culms. The pale slender structures are spike clusters, not individual blades. Photo does NOT resolve perigynium beak or stigma branches.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Spike position and drooping versus compact head architecture are quick Carex species clues.

part_examples.title: 3 · Compare one dense wetland fruiting head
part_examples.look_for: See many packed outward-pointing spiky structures forming one dense cylindrical head. This is quite different from Cherokee sedge's separate longer drooping spikes.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Head architecture narrows the group before small perigynium details.

part_examples.title: 4 · Compare narrow woodland leaves
part_examples.look_for: The low tuft with fine green leaves is cedar sedge. A blade cross-section is needed to prove its V-shaped/revolute margins; the broad face alone only teaches size and habit.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Separates a small dry calcareous woodland tuft from large wet bank sedges.

part_examples.title: 5 · Recognize Texas sedge in landscape
part_examples.look_for: The fine-textured clumps at the Austin botanical garden show expected small sedge stature. The sign is a photo subject label, not diagnostic fruiting proof.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Size and setting can start the key, but you still need the tiny fruiting spikes.

part_examples.title: 6 · Read a historical botanical plate
part_examples.role: historic illustration whole plant and fruit
part_examples.look_for: This is explicitly a DRAWING, not a real photograph. Use it to visualize separate spike arrangement, leaves and schematic enlarged flower/fruit parts; don't pretend it's a measured living macro.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Historic illustrations help decode parts when the local exact-species macro is missing.

part_examples.title: 7 · NEED PHOTO — perigynium and hidden achene
part_examples.look_for: At 1–2 mm scale, photograph one mature female Carex spikelet: show the subtending PISTILLATE SCALE separately from the enclosing PERIGYNIUM and cut/dissect a second perigynium to reveal the single ACHENE inside.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The unique sac-like perigynium is the most important structure defining Carex among local sedges.

part_examples.title: 8 · NEED PHOTO — Britton's sedge white wings
part_examples.look_for: Find a rights-cleared photograph of verified C. tetrastachya, preferably a 1–2 mm fruit macro showing silvery-white flat broad WINGS of perigynia and 2–4 separate rounded spikes. Do not substitute a different Carex species.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The wide white perigynium wings are one of the cleanest splits within these ten learner species.

part_examples.title: 9 · NEED PHOTO — canyon pair bases and leaf sections
part_examples.role: edwardsiana vs planostachys purple red culm base and leaf cross sections
part_examples.look_for: Same-angle exact-species photos of C. edwardsiana red-purple culm bases, widely separated spikes, and nearby C. planostachys narrow V-keeled or revolute leaves with mm ruler. Rights-cleared originals required.
part_examples.why_it_matters: This is the key Central Texas dry woodland pair where garden-like clump appearance is insufficient.
